title: Support for `IN` clause in streaming SQL
body:
## Description
Dozer streaming SQL does not currently support the `IN` operator. We need to extend support for `IN` with the following formats:

### Lookup from a static list of values
```
SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_name
WHERE column_name IN (value1, value2, ...);
```
This is pretty straightforward. Whenever an `Operation` is received, the value must be looked up from the list of static values provided in the SQL. 

The behavior is similar to an equality condition. The following table explains how the `WHERE` operator handles messages:

- `INSERT`: The insert message is propagated if the WHERE condition is matched
- `UPDATE`: The previous and new values must be evaluated against the condition:
    - If both the previous value and current value do not match the condition, no action is taken
    - If both the previous value and current value match, the UPDATE is propagated downstream
    - If the previous value does not match, but the new values match, an INSERT is propagated downstream
    - If the previous value matches, but the new value does not match, a DELETE is propagated downstream
- `DELETE`: The insert message is propagated if the WHERE condition is matched

### Lookup from an inner `SELECT`:
```
SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_name
WHERE column_name IN (SELECT STATEMENT);
```
This case is more complex as the values of the inner SELECT can change. This can follow a similar behavior of a JOIN operator. Whenever an INSERT message is received for the inner SELECT, for example, a lookup of the parent table must be performed to emit the values that were not previously matched. This behavior is the same one implemented in the JOIN. For such a case, the DAG should be constructed using a JOIN operator.

@mediuminvader can provide more details about the JOIN implementation

title: [wildcard] Checked allocation: a heap budget for the checked subset

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Tier-0 today proves properties of *values*: what may cross a task boundary, what may alias, what may move. It proves nothing about *resources*. I propose checked allocation: a checked program carries a proven heap-allocation bound for its checked regions, and the checker rejects a program whose emitted Go can allocate past a declared budget inside the checked subset, with a named diagnostic and a fix-it, in the same fail-closed shape as O4.9 (an unprovable allocation is a rejection, never a silent pass). Budgets are compositional: every function gets an allocation summary (constant, linear in a named input length, or unbounded), summaries compose across calls and spawns the way sendability classes compose today, and GUARANTEES.md gains a row that states an allocation claim with evidence instead of inheriting one.

### Which assumption it breaks

The assumption that the checker's job ends at value safety, and that what a checked program costs in heap is Go's business. GUARANTEES.md row 17 says it plainly: memory on the Go side is "Go's GC, unchanged". Rows 10 to 16 then list resource-adjacent surfaces as "no claim", as if allocation were an exotic primitive. It is not exotic. I measured the accepted side of the project's own corpus (139 verdict-pinned programs, main b1627e8): of the 47 ACCEPT and ACCEPT-MANAGED programs, 24 (51 percent) use at least one construct whose heap allocation is data-dependent and bounded by no claim anywhere: map literals in 15, append growth in 6, make with a runtime length in 5, string concatenation in 2. Half of what wears the "checked" badge allocates an amount nobody has stated, let alone proven. The emitted Go tells the same story from the other side: all 47 programs emit cleanly, 42 of them emit at least one allocation site, 126 sites in total (37 make, 10 append, 79 fmt.Sprintf, because Hybrid string interpolation lowers to Sprintf), and not one of those sites carries a stated bound. The sacred cow is the sentence "the claim is about value sharing, not resources" (row 12's scope note, applied everywhere). This proposal kills it for the one resource that actually kills checked programs in production: heap growth and the GC pressure that follows it.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Every current guarantee answers "can this value hurt me?" None answers "can this checked program blow up my heap?" For exactly the settings where a race-free checked subset is most attractive (embedded, edge, serverless, tight containers), allocation is the failure mode that remains after data races are gone: GC pauses, OOM kills, tail-latency blowups from a map that grew past the plan. A post-hoc profiler cannot fix this compositionally; it sees one run, not the space of runs. The Hybrid checker is the only component that can: it already runs dataflow over loans, origins and sendability classes, so allocation summaries ride an existing compositional engine instead of a new one. This is also not W-024 and not W-014. W-024 (escape-certified stack regions) is a lowering optimization for one loop-local shape; it makes a program cheaper and issues no verdict and no guarantee. W-014 (off-heap slabs) changes the runtime representation. Checked allocation changes neither lowering nor representation: it is a *verdict plus a claim*, a program outside its budget is rejected with a teaching diagnostic, and row 17 stops being an inheritance and becomes a claim with a corpus behind it, the same move W-016 made when it turned row 5's escape into a fourth check-site.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

M1, preregistered before any code: an allocation model for the checked subset. Enumerate the allocation sources in emitted Go (escaping composite literals, append growth, map literals and inserts, make with runtime length, string conversion and concatenation, interface boxing, closure captures), and a budget language of three summary forms: constant, linear in a named input, unbounded. Anything the model cannot summarize is unbounded by definition, never optimistically constant.

M2: an independent measurer against the model, run on the 47 ACCEPT-side corpus programs (the differential loop already executes the accept side byte-exact, so the harness exists). A pilot I ran while preparing this proposal confirms the static half is mechanical: hyb emits Go for all 47 accept-side programs and the allocation sites are enumerable in the output (126 sites, counted with a small script I can share); the dynamic half is the instrumentation described next. Instrument allocation with runtime MemStats deltas and testing.AllocsPerRun across at least three input sizes per program. The model passes only if both hold: (a) soundness: no program the model certifies as bounded ever measures above its certified bound at any tested input size; one exceedance falsifies the model, not the measurement. (b) usefulness: the model certifies, with no annotations, at least half of the ACCEPT-side programs that use no data-dependent construct, plus at least one program whose bound is genuinely linear (an append or map program with a provable cap). If (b) fails, the honest conclusion is that a plain profiler delivers the practical benefit and the language-level ROI hypothesis is dead; that result, with the full measurement table, is the published learning. Predictor cost is reported against current check time on the same corpus.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

The admitted subset shrinks, and I will not pretend otherwise. Unbounded append or map growth inside a checked region would need a budget annotation or the managed hatch, so some programs that pass today will reject; that is a new false-rejection class and it needs the same governance the project already uses for verdict changes (VERDICTS.md amendments, the section 9.7 tripwire discipline). Input-dependent bounds need a vocabulary ("linear in len(x)") that SPEC does not have today, and interprocedural summaries will complicate hy-check. There is also a real chance the maintainers judge the guarantee worth less than the subset it costs. That judgment is theirs; what this proposal guarantees them is the measurement table to make it with, which nobody has today.

### Track terms

- [x] I understand no prototype is required and failure-with-knowledge is a valid, paid outcome
- [x] I understand all outcomes (including declines and failures) are published in MOONSHOT.md

title: [wildcard] Publication-authority regions: checked parallel intent plans with aggregate obligations

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

AI-assisted research by Toyol Digital, human-operated. Introduce opt-in publication-authority regions. Parallel tasks compute typed intents rather than external effects. Each receives immutable grants specifying stable identity, permitted resources and operations, and individual allowances. The parent validates the complete batch after joining all workers, returning a canonical valid plan or rejection. The initial subset excludes foreign I/O, shared mutable state, clocks, random inputs, inter-worker communication and unbounded spawning. External execution remains outside Tier-0.

### Which assumption it breaks

GUARANTEES.md establishes checked value-sharing and loan safety, not authority to perform effects or satisfaction of aggregate cross-task constraints. Race-free execution can still produce an invalid effect plan. We propose a distinct checked publication boundary, preserving existing task semantics elsewhere.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

The research question is whether a compiler can prevent publication of invalid plans when individually permitted intents collectively exceed a global constraint. Parallel index builders may each satisfy a local quota while exceeding a common allowance. Unlike ordinary deterministic folding, the entire plan is accepted or rejected before publication. Related work: #2475 Kahn determinism and #2815 falsifier; #2385 commutative capsules and ordered folds; #417 and #634 transactional shared state; #2620 durable continuations. Ordered folding is not our novelty. The distinct contribution is authority and aggregate validation without shared transactional cells or external effects. We acknowledge established capability and effect-system prior art; a shared evaluation is preferable if maintainers consider this an extension of #2385.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Actual standalone Go 1.23.2 prototype: go test -race -count=1 -v ./... passed four tests. All six permutations of three intents produce identical canonical output with cap 10; all six reject with cap 9. Seven invalid cases reject wrong resources, duplicate identities, missing workers, excess individual allowances, zero units, unknown identities and duplicate resources. Compiler integration has not been implemented. Proposed M1: preregister stable identities, typed grants, canonical encoding, deterministic rejection, and transitive purity. Proposed M2: implement source-to-plan lowering and an independent verifier for two Hybrid fork/join examples; test 20 positive/negative programs and 100 forced schedules with GOMAXPROCS 1,2,4. A single invalid published plan, differing canonical outcome, or hidden external effect falsifies the claim. Measure time and allocation against an equivalent sequential validator. Publish counterexamples and negative results.

Requires typed effects, transitive purity checks, immutable grants and checked lowering. The admitted subset may be too narrow. If an ordinary Go validator delivers equivalent practical benefit without compiler changes, the language-level ROI hypothesis fails. No claim of external atomicity, rollback, exactly-once execution, crash recovery or general liveness. Initial tests are standalone evidence, not a formal proof or completed Hybrid implementation.

title: registerUser access token can reference a different user id
body:
## Bug

`registerUser()` currently builds the returned `id` and the JWT `sub` with two separate `Date.now()` calls. If time advances between those calls, the API can return one user id while signing an access token for a different subject. Downstream authenticated requests would then identify a different user than the one returned by registration.

## Expected fix

Generate the new user id once, return that id, and sign the access token with the same id as `sub`. Add a regression test that forces the timestamp to advance between calls and verifies the token subject matches the returned id.

## Scope

This issue is limited to the registration response/token subject mismatch in `apps/api/src/services/authService.js` plus focused API service test coverage.

title: UI for Database Connection Add and Delete
body:
The goal of this ticket is to add a basic UI to add and delete new database destinations. This will be done purely in SvelteKit. The backend endpoints are already implemented in Go, though you may need to make small changes or fixes.

## How to Run

1. Run the backend: `go run .`
2. Run the frontend in a separate terminal: `cd frontend; npm run dev`
3. Go to `http://localhost:8080/login` to log into the dashboard
4. Then you should be able to go to `http://localhost:5173/dashboard` to run the sveltekit app

## Requirements

- Everything should be implemented using plain HTML. There is no need to implement any CSS or styling.
- The UI is a single-page-app which makes ajax calls to our backend in Go.
- The pull request will be against the `svelte-2` branch, _not main_

### Part 1: Delete 

1. If you go to this page, there is a delete button: http://localhost:5173/dashboard/connections/
2. When the user clicks delete, we should show a confirmation asking if they are sure. The dialog should use this UI element: https://shoelace.style/components/dialog
3. If the user clicks OK, then make a `DELETE` fetch request to `/api/destinations/{id}`.
4. If the deletion is successful, then show a success alert, otherwise show the error. Use this component for showing alerts: https://shoelace.style/components/alert

### Part 2: Add

 The user should be able to add new connections.

#### Show Form

1. Navigate to this page: `http://localhost:5173/dashboard/connections/new/duckdb/`
2. This should make an ajax request to `/api/destinations/params/[type]` where `type` is a SvelteKit url parameter
3. That ajax endpoint will return a list of form fields:
    - name: the name of the field
    - type: the type of form field. It could be text, textarea, password, number, or bool (checkbox)
    - label: the label for the field
    - default: a default value

Here is an example:

```
{
    "form_fields": [
        {
            "name": "database",
            "type": "text",
            "label": "Database Name",
            "default": ""
        },
        {
            "name": "token",
            "type": "password",
            "label": "MotherDuck Token",
            "default": ""
        }
    ],
    "type": "DuckDB"
}
```

4. Using this data, show a form on the page with all of these fields.
5. Additionally, have a form field for the "Name" of the destination
6. Finally, there should be a "save" button

#### Save Data

1. When the user clicks the save button, make an ajax `POST /destinations`
2. The payload should look like this:

```
{
  "type": [type from URL],
  "name": "user-entered name",
  "settings": {
    "database": "user-entered-db-value",
    "token": "user-entered-token-value"
  }
}
```

3. If the POST is successful, then redirect the user to `/dashboard/connections` 
4. If the POST fails, then show an alert with the error returned from the API.

#### Testing

This should work with the following four URLs:

1. http://localhost:5173/dashboard/connections/new/duckdb/
2. http://localhost:5173/dashboard/connections/new/clickhouse/
3. http://localhost:5173/dashboard/connections/new/bigquery/
5. http://localhost:5173/dashboard/connections/new/postgres/
6. http://localhost:5173/dashboard/connections/new/redshift/
